title: {0, 1/2}-Chvátal-Gomory cuts
contribution: Shows that separating {0,1/2}-Chvátal-Gomory cuts is a minimum-weight binary clutter problem, NP-hard in general and polynomial for edge-path-of-a-tree structures, and that weakening the rows with the variable bounds gives a polynomially separable family containing many known facet classes.
problem_entry: The closure P_1/2 depends on the describing system (A, b), not only on P (p. 2); it characterises totally unimodular and balanced matrices (Theorems 1-2, p. 2) and contains many facet classes (p. 3); the question is posed as the separation problem {0,1/2}-SEP (p. 3).
key_idea: Violation depends only on parities and slacks: a violated cut exists iff min{s*^T u : u in F(A,b)} < 1 (pp. 5-6), which is the minimum-weight binary clutter problem (Theorem 3, p. 6); rows are weakened with the bounds to at most two odd coefficients and separated as minimum-weight odd cycles (Theorems 4-6, pp. 7-10).
assumptions: Pure integer systems with integer A and b, P_I != P, an odd coefficient in every row (p. 1); bounds 0 <= x <= d taken as rows for the weakening (p. 9); applications are polytopes (clique partitioning, ATSP, plant location, acyclic subgraph, linear ordering), no instance library (pp. 10-15).
proof_devices: Camion's theorem: a square submatrix with even row and column sums and entry sum not divisible by four yields a half-integral point and a {0,1/2} multiplier vector separating P from P_1/2 (Theorem 1); same construction on an odd-order submatrix with row and column sums two (Theorem 2), p. 2
Parity reformulation: violation depends only on (A,b) mod 2 and the slack s* = b - Ax*, violated cut iff min{s*^T u : u in F(A,b)} < 1, pp. 5-6
Two-way reduction with the minimum-weight binary clutter problem, the reverse one building a system and point whose slack equals the clutter weights (Theorem 3, Corollary 1), p. 6

Binary-clutter representation through fundamental cycles and cuts of a graph and tree: separation becomes a minimum-weight odd cycle (Theorem 4, p. 7) or a minimum-weight odd cut via Padberg-Rao (Theorem 5, p. 8)
Instance reductions (a)-(d): slack >= 1 rows dropped, least-slack copy of duplicates, components of the row intersection graph, tight unit rows eliminated, pp. 6-7
L-, U-, LU-weakening to at most two odd coefficients per row; an O(n) dynamic programme picks the two minimum-slack weakenings (even and odd right-hand side) per triple (Theorem 6), pp. 8-10

Known facet classes re-derived as {0,1/2}-combinations of weakened rows: 2-chorded odd cycle, odd wheel, weak odd CAT, plant-location odd cycle, Möbius ladder, and a new acyclic-subgraph class, pp. 10-15
experiments: none: no implementation; the only computational statement points to Fischetti and Toth (1994), where weak odd CAT inequalities sped up an ATSP branch-and-cut on hard real-world instances (p. 12)
positioning: Presents Theorems 4-5 as generalising the Gerards-Schrijver and Padberg-Rao polynomial cases (pp. 7-8, 16); re-derives classes of Grötschel-Wakabayashi, Chopra-Rao, Balas and Grötschel-Jünger-Reinelt instead of criticising them (pp. 10-15); thanks Gerards for the binary-clutter link (p. 16).
writing: Six-section theorem-proof paper with the contribution in the abstract (p. 1); light, explicit hedging ('To our knowledge', pp. 10, 14; 'hopefully gives a tight approximation', p. 10); conclusions close on one lesson sentence (p. 16), an early case of Heuristic 7 (close with a lesson).
limits_future: NP-hard in general (p. 6); the weakened family is a subclass whose tightness is hoped for, not measured (p. 10); separation complexity of lifted odd CAT and comb inequalities left open (p. 12); heuristic cycle-length cap for the acyclic subgraph polytope (p. 14); nothing implemented or tested; no future-work section.

method_links.note: The cut-loop sub-decision (which cut to add) is written as an optimisation over CG multipliers with the slack as cost (p. 6), the formulation that the later MIP separation over the first Chvátal closure hands to a general-purpose solver (SKILL.md Method 6 practice; card D003, pp. 3-4). Here it is attacked by complexity theory and combinatorial algorithms on a weakened system; no solver appears.
The reflex of one separation routine per facet class is reversed, but as a closing lesson drawn from the results, not as the study's starting hypothesis.
An early case: the conclusions end on an 'An outcome of the research' lesson sentence.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Separate over the derivation, not over the class
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Separation over {0,1/2} multipliers of the (weakened) original rows instead of a template per facet class; known classes re-derived; the conclusions turn this into a lesson. S009 (p. 6) derives its 2-matching inequalities the same way.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Weaken the source rows until the separation oracle is polynomial
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: L-, U- and LU-weakening with the variable bounds down to at most two odd coefficients per row; two minimum-slack weakenings per triple by an O(n) dynamic programme; polynomial optimisation over the closure of the weakened system (Theorem 6).

transferable: Check whether a restricted-multiplier closure depends on the polyhedron or on its description before trying to strengthen it by reformulation (p. 2).
For a CG family with fixed denominator q, work with (A, b) mod q and the slack vector: a violated cut exists iff the minimum slack over admissible parity vectors is below 1 (pp. 5-6).
Shrink a separation instance by slack, duplicate-row, connected-component and tight-bound reductions before solving it (pp. 6-7).

With at most two odd coefficients per row, separate by a minimum-weight odd cycle (slacks as weights, right-hand-side parities as labels); otherwise weaken rows with the bounds first and keep, per triple, only the two minimum-slack weakenings found by an O(n) dynamic programme (pp. 7-10).
Re-derive known facet classes as {0,1/2}-combinations of weakened base inequalities: it explains them and gives a polynomial separation for a superclass (pp. 10-15).
To show a closure is strictly weaker than integrality, build a half-integral point and a {0,1/2} multiplier vector on a forbidden submatrix (Camion) (p. 2).
coauthors: A Caprara (DEIS, Bologna); Fischetti's printed affiliation DIE, University of L'Aquila (p. 1)

quotes.text: An outcome of the research is that separation sometimes becomes easier if one does not insist in detecting violated cuts belonging to a restricted (and sometimes complicated) class of inequalities, but concentrates on the way these cuts can be derived from the original formulation.

The computational experience reported in Fischetti and Toth (1994) has shown that these inequalities are useful to speed-up the convergence of a branch-and-cut algorithm for solving hard ATS real-world instances.

title: A branch-and-cut algorithm for the symmetric generalized traveling salesman problem
contribution: A branch-and-cut code for the symmetric (E-)GTSP that turns the companion paper's facets into exact and heuristic separation routines, adds a Lagrangian root, a core with pricing and branching on cuts, and solves 53 instances of up to 442 nodes to optimality.
problem_entry: The natural x-y model relies on the integrality of y and has a very poor LP relaxation (Figure 1.1, p. 4); the companion paper's facets are turned into separation routines and a branch-and-cut (pp. 1, 4-8).
key_idea: Padberg-Rinaldi-style branch-and-cut with max-flow GSEC separation, exact when max y* = 1 (pp. 8-11), a heuristic GSEC_H2 returning a nested family of cuts per round (pp. 12-14), a Lagrangian 1-tree root on the shrunken cluster graph (pp. 21-23), a core with pricing (pp. 23-24) and branching on parity cuts over cluster unions (pp. 24-25); E-GTSP is polynomial for a fixed number of clusters (p. 18).
assumptions: Pure 0-1 x-y model; E-GTSP with integer triangular costs implemented (p. 19); m >= 5 for the polyhedral results (p. 5); TSPLIB instances with 48-442 nodes clustered by a fully specified farthest-centre generator (m = ceil(n/5)), plus natural and grid clusterings and two geographic instances (pp. 25-26, 28).
proof_devices: Dominance of violation degrees: a node s of maximal y* can always play node i, so n-1 max-flows suffice for (2.3), p. 9; with y*_s = 1, n+m-2 max-flows give a most violated GSEC, p. 10
Flow reversal: one s-j flow gives a feasible s-v flow of value f_v + min{f_v, f_j - f_v}, a lower bound on every max-flow from s, p. 10
Matroid argument from the spanning-tree case: the active subtour constraints form a nested family covering all nodes, which motivates GSEC_H2, pp. 12-13
Lagrangian subproblem as a min-cost 1-tree on the shrunken cluster graph, p. 22; root rows chosen so that the first LP bound is at least the Lagrangian bound, pp. 22-23
Layered network: best E-GTSP tour for a fixed cluster sequence by |C_h1| shortest paths, hence polynomial for fixed m, O((m-1)! n^3), p. 18
Pricing cost bookkeeping: row-by-row O(|E| + nq + sum |J_i|) against column-by-column O(|E'| q), with O(n^2) memory, p. 24
experiments: C code, HP 9000/700 and DECstation 5000/240, CPLEX 2.1 as LP solver (p. 25); 53 instances (two geographic plus TSPLIB 48-442) and 42 under grid clusterings (pp. 33-36); all 53 solved, about 70% without branching, the Lagrangian UB optimal on 30 (56.6%), the 11.7% Lagrangian LB gap traced to the simplified model's slack (pp. 27-28); TS225 with grid clustering mu = 5 unsolved after 100,000 s (p. 36); time = alpha n^beta with beta = 3.99 total (p. 29); no rival compared, single runs, parameters from computational experience with no named tuning set (p. 19).
positioning: Branch-and-cut credited to Padberg-Rinaldi and Jünger-Reinelt-Rinaldi (p. 19); GSEC_H2 'an improved version' of Grötschel and Holland's heuristic (p. 13); Lagrangian loops in the Held-Karp spirit (p. 22); prior GTSP work listed but neither criticised nor compared (pp. 2-3).
writing: Pascal-like procedures (pp. 10-14, 19-20, 26); parameter values given with '(say)' (p. 19); hedged design choices (depth-first, p. 25) but firm summaries ('quite satisfactory', p. 29); no conclusions section, the text ends with a regression (p. 29).
limits_future: Exact GSEC routine exact only when max y* = 1 (p. 11); exact generalized 2-matching separation too slow, heuristics only (p. 14); row-by-row pricing needs O(n^2) memory (p. 24); depth-first not best in general (p. 25); poor Lagrangian LB (p. 27); TS225 under grid clustering unsolved (p. 36); no future directions.

method_links.note: A cut loop that adds the individually most violated cuts needs many iterations (spanning-tree argument), so GSEC_H2 returns a nested family spanning the graph per round. The cure changes what the separator returns per round, not the point the loop separates.

What lives in the LP is decided by density and bound, not by a variable's role: y kept for sparsity, projected out only in the Lagrangian model, whose LP bound (basic-LB) is measured and found slack; most edge columns kept out by a core and pricing; intra-cluster edges dropped for E-GTSP.
Dated (1995): a single code judged against the optimum with no rival; parameter settings from computational experience with no named tuning set; branching on cuts called superior without a table.
Dated: no conclusions section, no lesson and no status label; the text ends with a regression on running times.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Dual information steers the primal side
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lagrangian tours on the shrunken graph refined by RP2; the LP's edges at 1 completed by nearest insertion; zero Lagrangian reduced costs seed the core edge set. Also in S009 (pp. 14, 16) and S012 (pp. 10, 17).

Core from zero Lagrangian reduced costs plus the 5 cheapest edges per node; at most 100 columns per round; separation only after all columns price out; reduced-cost removal and fixing; row-by-row pricing. Also in S009 (pp. 15-16) and S012 (p. 11).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Separation cascade with early exit, exact separator last as an audit
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Pool, fans, two heuristics, decreasing violation thresholds 0.1/0.01/0.001, then exact max-flow; exit at the first stage with cuts; the exact routine found cuts only on 45TS225 (9 cuts). Also in S009 (p. 16).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Measure the relaxed model's slack apart from the subgradient's error
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: basic-LB, the LP bound of the simplified model, is reported next to the Lagrangian LB and shows that the 11.7% gap is the model's slack.

transferable: Look for a polynomial special case inside a heuristic that fixes one of two entangled decisions (layered network for a fixed cluster sequence, p. 18).
Specify instance generators completely, tie-breaking included, and test sensitivity with a second generator (pp. 25-26, 28).

Order separation from cheap to exact (pool, fans in O(mn + |E*|), spanning-forest heuristic, cluster max-flow heuristic, lower thresholds 0.1/0.01/0.001, exact max-flow last) and stop at the first stage that returns cuts (pp. 19-21).
Return a nested family per separation round: add fractional edges in Kruskal order and test the cut of every merged component (pp. 12-14).
Seed the root LP with the rows active in the best Lagrangian solution, so the first LP bound is at least the Lagrangian bound (pp. 22-23).
Price columns row by row when rows are sparse and many columns must be priced (p. 24); hash each cut's compact form into 4 bytes for duplicate tests (p. 21).
Branch on a parity cut x(delta(S)) <= 2k or >= 2k+2 with S built from consecutive clusters of the incumbent and chosen by a 2-exchange estimate of the cost increase (pp. 24-25).

Report the relaxed model's LP bound beside the Lagrangian bound (p. 27), the exact separator's hit count after the heuristics (p. 28), and a fitted exponent per time component, time = alpha n^beta (p. 29).
coauthors: JJ Salazar González (DEIOC, La Laguna), P Toth (DEIS, Bologna); Fischetti's printed affiliation DEI, University of Padova (p. 1)

quotes.text: Therefore, a cutting plane SST algorithm that adds violated cuts chosen only on the basis of their individual degree of violation, is likely to require a high number of iterations before producing the optimal family of cuts.
We next describe some important implementation issues, including the best parameter setting resulting from our computational experience.

title: Algorithms for railway crew management
contribution: An overview of modelling options for railway crew scheduling and rostering and of the two codes the authors built for Ferrovie dello Stato (the Lagrangian set-covering heuristic CFT and a rostering relaxation with a bound-driven constructive heuristic), tested in FS's FASTER and FARO competitions; every number is unreadable in this text.
problem_entry: Application-driven: FS's very large crew problems under deregulation (p. 1), decomposed as in practice into crew scheduling and crew rostering (pp. 3-4); FS promoted research on very large set covering, which led to the joint project (p. 9).
key_idea: Choose the model by where the feasibility rules live (set partitioning for scheduling, arc-based for rostering, p. 8); relax partitioning to covering and keep only maximal duties (p. 9); CFT: Lagrangian scores from several near-optimal multipliers, fixing, iteration and a non-frozen core with pricing (pp. 10-11); rostering bound by an assignment problem plus scalar subproblems and a bound-driven constructive heuristic (pp. 14-17).
assumptions: Covering the nodes of a graph by circuits; the arc model needs additive costs and is weak under tight rules (p. 6); set partitioning is tighter but huge (p. 8); pure set covering for scheduling, beyond exact codes at FS size (p. 9); FS competition data, FASTER and FARO (pp. 11, 18); all numeric rules unreadable (pp. 12-14).
proof_devices: v(RP), in minutes, always equals an integer number of days, so r is a lower bound on the number of weeks, p. 16
Lagrangian decomposition of RP into an assignment problem plus scalar r and z subproblems; two assignment problems give a tight bound, pp. 16-17
Lagrangian SCP subproblem solved by the sign of the Lagrangian costs, p. 10
experiments: Table 1 (FASTER: trips, duties, density, lower bound, CFT value, best other value) and Table 2 (FARO: duties, simple and Lagrangian lower bounds, weeks, time) exist, but every number is unreadable (pp. 11-12, 18); stated outcomes: near-optimal SCP solutions in limited time and rostering instances solved to proven optimality (pp. 11, 18); baselines are other competitors' best solutions and a simple bound; no seeds or repeated runs.
positioning: Surveys crew management, exact and Lagrangian SCP methods (Balas and Ho onwards) and rostering (pp. 2, 9-10, 12); sets the railway case against airline and urban transit (pp. 4, 9, 12); defers details to the authors' reports (pp. 9, 14, 19).
writing: An overview ('we give an outline', p. 1); modelling advice framed as experience ('According to our experience', p. 8); firm claims about the tables; no conclusions section (p. 18).
limits_future: Decomposition is a compromise forced by difficulty and practice (p. 4); feedback between the phases suggested, not implemented (p. 4); the core definition is critical (p. 11); exact methods out of reach for scheduling (p. 9); no future work. Digits and punctuation lost in this extraction; re-OCR needed.

method_links.note: Steps 1-2: the model is chosen by where the feasibility rules of the instances live; dominated columns removed by the covering relaxation with inclusion-maximal duties, which 'considerably reduces the number of variables'; a non-frozen core with pricing keeps most columns out.

Dated, before the 2002-2009 general-purpose period: exact SCP codes ruled out by size and problem-specific Lagrangian codes built; no general-purpose solver, not even as a baseline. CFT's fixing phase is the hard fixing that local branching later replaced by soft fixing (SKILL.md, local-branching anatomy).
Application first: both codes answer FS competitions (FASTER, FARO) on FS data, and an FS author co-signs.
Dated: no conclusions section; the paper ends with the rostering results.

Precursor of step 4: the spread of greedy solutions over near-equivalent multipliers is exploited by running the heuristic for several of them; random perturbation in the rostering refinement; no seeds and no control arm.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Dual information steers the primal side
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lagrangian costs as greedy scores for set covering; the lower-bound increase as the roster-construction score. With S005 (pp. 22-24) and S009 (pp. 14, 16).

A core of low-Lagrangian-cost duties updated by pricing inside the subgradient optimisation, called 'one of the main ingredients for the success' of the scheme. With S005 (pp. 23-24) and S009 (pp. 15-16).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Relax partitioning to covering when over-cover is allowed, keep only maximal columns
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Crews may travel as passengers, so set covering replaces set partitioning and only inclusion-maximal duties among those of equal cost are generated.

transferable: Choose the formulation by where the feasibility rules live: set partitioning when circuits are short and their feasibility depends on the whole sequence, arc-based when the binding rules concern consecutive pairs (pp. 6-8).
Relax partitioning to covering when over-covering is allowed and generate only inclusion-maximal columns of equal cost (p. 9).

Score columns by Lagrangian costs from several near-optimal multiplier vectors and run the greedy from each, since near-equivalent multipliers give very different solutions and the bound does not predict their quality (pp. 10-11).
Iterate subgradient, heuristic and fixing phases on the shrinking instance, then refine; keep a core of low-Lagrangian-cost columns but update it by pricing (p. 11).
Split a sequencing bound with side counts into an assignment problem plus scalar subproblems by relaxing the counting constraints (pp. 16-17).
Repair a constructive solution by deleting its last, typically worst, components and rebuilding them with perturbed or retuned parameters (p. 17).
coauthors: A Caprara, P Toth, D Vigo (DEIS, Bologna), PL Guida (Ferrovie dello Stato SpA); Fischetti's printed affiliation DMI, University of Udine (p. 1)

quotes.text: the choice of the appropriate model and solution algorithm strongly depends on the particular structure of the problem in hand
The use of pricing within Lagrangian optimization drastically reduces computing time

title: Solving the orienteering problem through branch-and-cut
contribution: A branch-and-cut for the orienteering problem with new cycle-cover and path inequalities, cuts conditioned on the incumbent (conditional cuts, branch cover cuts) and a two-stage root scheme, solving instances of up to 500 nodes and more Class IV instances, with tighter root bounds, than the published branch-and-cut of Gendreau, Laporte and Semet.
problem_entry: TSP facet results do not transfer because the TSP and OP polytopes are disjoint when the time bound is active, so the paper enters computationally, with inequalities justified by their effect on the test bed (p. 5); prior heuristics, exact methods and one branch-and-cut are listed (p. 2).
key_idea: An x-y model plus logical, 2-matching, cover, cycle-cover and new path inequalities (pp. 3-8); conditional cuts valid for every solution better than the incumbent (p. 9); branch cover cuts cut off the support graph at the root, which is stored and solved later on the union graph with ordinary branching (pp. 17-18).
assumptions: Pure 0-1 model with integer nonnegative data, a feasible solution assumed, 2-cycles excluded (pp. 3-4); the time constraint read as a knapsack (p. 6); Classes I-IV from OP and VRP literature, TSPLIB under three prize generations and two rivals' random generators, t0 = ceil(alpha v(TSP)) (pp. 18-21).
proof_devices: Logical constraints leave y in {0, 1/2, 1} and exclude 1/2, so the integrality of y is redundant, p. 5
Validity of path inequalities by contradiction, following a violating solution along the path, pp. 7-8
Conditional-cut argument: x(T) <= y(V(T)) always holds, with equality only if the solution lies in T, so x(T) - y(V(T)) <= -1 is valid for improving solutions when none lies in T, p. 9
Simplifying overlapping teeth never decreases the violation, p. 11
A violated path inequality must lie in the support graph (sign argument), which bounds the enumeration, p. 11
Convergence of the two-stage scheme by inhibiting branch cover cuts in the second round, p. 17
Fractional points violating a new inequality and none of the earlier ones (Figures 2.1, 2.2), pp. 5, 7-8
experiments: C code, DECstation 5000/240 and HP 9000/720 (80 MHz, 59 SPECs), CPLEX 3.0, 18,000 s limit with %-UB as an error bound at the limit (pp. 18, 20); Class I 45 runs (1 at the limit), Class II 132 runs (10 at the limit), Class III 440 instances (5 unsolved), Class IV averages over 5 instances (pp. 21, 25-31); Laporte-Martello's own code rerun on n = 25 (0.1 s at alpha 0.2 up to more than 2 hours at 0.6, none solved at 0.8, p. 20); Gendreau-Laporte-Semet compared via published results with a Dongarra speed ratio of 1.8 and their averaging convention (pp. 21-22); Class II at alpha 0.25 and 0.75 not shown (p. 20); single runs.
positioning: Cycle-relaxation work of Balas and Bauer and Balas's Prize-Collecting TSP polyhedra as related (pp. 2, 5); Padberg-Rinaldi and Jünger-Reinelt-Rinaldi branch-and-cut (p. 15); heuristic 'along the same lines' as Ramesh and Brown 'but uses LP information to guide the search' (p. 14); direct rival Gendreau-Laporte-Semet (pp. 21-22); 'compares favourably with previous published methods' (p. 1).
writing: Coins 'conditional cuts' and 'branch cover cut' (pp. 9, 17); hedged design claims ('hopefully violated', p. 10; 'although does not dominate', p. 18) next to firm summaries ('quite satisfactory', p. 21); an early version at EURO XIII 1994 (p. 3); no conclusions section (p. 22).
limits_future: No polyhedral analysis (p. 5); a branch cover cut may cut off the optimum, repaired by the second stage (p. 17); enumeration unlikely to complete on dense support graphs (p. 17); first-stage tailing off (p. 18); time-limit instances in Classes I-III (pp. 21, 25-29); Class IV harder (p. 22); no future directions.

method_links.note: The sub-decision whether a better solution lies inside the current support is answered by solving that restricted instance exactly: enumeration under a time limit, and the same branch-and-cut on the union of the stored support graphs. The code is its own subroutine on a restricted instance, the shape of later neighbourhood sub-MIPs (inference; the text makes no such link).
The second stage works on a thinned instance, the union of the root's support graphs, kept exact by the branch cover argument; the LP starts from a small edge core grown by pricing.

The root loop is redesigned where it stalls: a branch cover cut instead of branching when separation fails; tailing off met by a bound-improvement rule (0.001 in 10 iterations) and by branching after 5 branch cover cuts. The separators stay; the cut-or-branch decision changes.

Dated: one rival rerun with its own code on the authors' machine and the rivals' generators used for their classes; the other compared through published results from another machine scaled by a speed ratio, with its averaging convention adopted, the form the skill records as a 2017 lapse; alpha 0.25 and 0.75 summarised as comparable but not shown; the two-stage claim has no table.
Talk first: an early version was presented at EURO XIII, Glasgow, July 1994, a large conference rather than a small workshop; no single-instance traces precede the tables.
Dated: no conclusions section and no lesson; the paper ends with the Class IV comparison.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Conditional cuts: any inequality satisfied by every feasible solution better than LB may be added; the family x(T) - y(V(T)) <= -1 with T = E(S) and p(S) <= LB from max-flow sets, or with T the support graph after enumerating it within a time limit.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Exclude a region by one cut, store it, solve it later
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Branch cover cuts cut off the current support graph at the root; the union of the stored graphs is solved afterwards with ordinary branching, which keeps the method exact; the same shape as the 2003 local-branching scheme read as exact strategic branching in SKILL.md Common Misreading 5 (inference).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Dual information steers the primal side
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: LP values w_e := x*_e guide the two-stage heuristic, run every fifth separation. With S005 (pp. 22-24) and S012 (pp. 10, 17).
First LP with all y, the heuristic's edges and the 5 cheapest edges per node; at most 100 columns per pricing round; purging and root fixing by reduced cost. With S005 (pp. 23-24) and S012 (p. 11).
Pool, logical, GSEC, 2-matching, cover, path, conditional, leaving at the first family that yields cuts. With S005 (pp. 19-21).

transferable: Conditional cuts: any inequality satisfied by every feasible solution better than the incumbent may be added; for x(T) - y(V(T)) <= -1 it suffices that T contains no solution with value above LB, e.g. T = E(S) with p(S) <= LB (p. 9).
Harvest conditional cuts from max-flow separation by testing the source side of each minimum cut for p(S) <= LB (pp. 10, 13).

Branch cover cuts: when separation fails at the root, cut off the support graph, store it and continue; finish by solving the union of the stored graphs with branch cover cuts disabled, which guarantees convergence (pp. 17-18).
Max-flow GSEC separation by decreasing y*, raising the capacity of edge [1, v] after each hit and reading two minimum cuts from every max-flow (p. 10).

Separate knapsack covers by solving the knapsack with the variables at 0 or 1 fixed, then make the cover minimal greedily before extending it (p. 12); enumerate path inequalities inside the support graph with backtracking (pp. 11-12).

Run an LP-guided heuristic every fifth separation with w_e := x*_e (pp. 14, 16); strong-branch on 15 candidates scored 0.75 UB0 + 0.25 UB1 (pp. 17-18); branch when the bound gains less than 0.001 in 10 rounds (p. 16).

Rerun rivals' own codes and generators where possible, and state any conversion of published times and the averaging convention; at a time limit, treat the best value as optimal and print %-UB as an upper bound on the error (pp. 20-22).
coauthors: JJ Salazar González (DEIOC, La Laguna), P Toth (DEIS, Bologna); Fischetti's printed affiliation DEI, University of Padova (p. 1)

quotes.text: We next address inequalities that are not guaranteed to be valid for our problem, but can nevertheless be used in a cutting plane context.
Our computational experience shows that the overall scheme typically performs better than (although does not dominate) the classical one.
